match.reason: No bank point teaches how words from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages or Aboriginal English carry cultural knowledge; the closest, soc-language-culture, is a Year 11 Society and Culture card on language and culture in general, at a different depth and subject, so a new point is needed.

rejected.title: Language and cultural knowledge
card: Words from a particular language can carry cultural knowledge and a way of seeing the world. A single word may hold ideas that English needs a whole sentence to explain.
Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Languages have words tied to Country, kinship and community. Such a word can show how people understand their relationships to land and to each other.
Aboriginal English is a variety of English used by many Aboriginal people. It can carry its own expressions, meanings and ways of telling stories.

When a writer uses these languages in a text, they pass on meaning that English alone may not hold. A reader may need context or a glossary to understand a word, but the word still keeps its own meaning.
rejected.remember: A word from a language can carry cultural knowledge that a plain English swap may not hold.

a.q: Why might a writer keep an Aboriginal language word in a story instead of using an English word?
opts: The word carries cultural meaning English may not hold
The word makes the story easier for all readers to follow
The word shows the writer could not find an English word
The word is only there to make the text sound unusual
a.why: A word from an Aboriginal language can carry knowledge and a way of seeing that English may not hold, so the writer keeps it to pass that meaning on. It does not always make reading easier, and a reader may need context to understand it.
a.clue: Think about what the word holds that a swap might lose.

b.q: A poet writes about her grandmother's Country and uses a word from her family's language for the bond between people and land. She adds no direct English swap. What does this choice most likely do?
opts: It passes on a cultural idea that English may not fully hold
It shows that the poet's English vocabulary is limited
It makes the poem's meaning the same as a plain English line
It hides the poem's meaning so that no reader can grasp it
b.why: Keeping the word lets the poem pass on a cultural way of seeing the bond with land. Readers can still find meaning through context. The meaning is not the same as a plain English line, because English may not hold all of it.
b.clue: Ask what the word keeps that an English swap might lose.

version.title: Language and cultural knowledge
card: A word from a particular language can carry cultural knowledge and a way of seeing the world. English may need a whole sentence, or more, to explain it.
Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Languages have words for kinship, Country and community. A kinship word can name a relationship and the duties that come with it.
Aboriginal English, a dialect spoken by many Aboriginal people, carries meanings of its own too. Deadly, for example, means excellent.
When writers use these words, they pass on meaning that English alone may not hold. A reader may need context or a glossary, but the word keeps its full meaning.
version.remember: A swap into plain English can lose the cultural knowledge a word carries.

a.q: Why might a writer use a word from an Aboriginal language in a story rather than an English word?
opts: It holds cultural meaning that English may not hold
It makes the story quicker for every reader to follow
It shows the writer did not know the English word
It adds an unusual sound, with no meaning beyond that
a.why: The word can carry knowledge and a way of seeing that an English swap may lose, so keeping it passes that meaning on. It may make reading slower, not quicker, since a reader may need context.
a.clue: What might be lost in a swap into English?

b.q: A Torres Strait Islander poet uses a word from her language for a relative, and the poem shows the duties that come with that relationship. Why not just write "aunt"?
opts: Aunt may miss the duties the word carries in her culture
Aunt would make the poem harder for readers to follow
Aunt holds more meaning than the word in her language
Aunt names a relationship that English speakers lack
b.why: A kinship word can name a relationship and the duties that come with it, which aunt may not hold. Keeping the word passes on that cultural knowledge. Aunt would be easier for most readers, not harder, but it would lose meaning.
b.clue: What does the poem show comes with the relationship?
